lessons.title: Arms of government, separation of powers and checks and balances

steps.title: Three jobs in one school
steps.display: Prefects enforce rules  |  Student council writes rules  |  Principal judges disputes
working: No single person writes, enforces, and judges the same rule.
Splitting the three jobs keeps everyone fair.
steps.narration: In your school, the council writes rules, prefects enforce them, and the principal settles fights. Splitting those three jobs stops one person from becoming a bully.

steps.title: The legislature makes laws and watches public funds
steps.display: Section 4: National Assembly (Senate + House of Representatives) and State Houses of Assembly
working: Senate: 3 Senators per State and 1 from the FCT (s. 48); House of Reps: 360 members (s. 49).
Passes bills into law (s. 58), approves spending from the Consolidated Revenue Fund (ss. 80–81), and investigates public agencies (s. 88).
steps.narration: First comes the law-making team, because every rule must start somewhere. Think of a family meeting deciding house rules and pocket money. In Nigeria, the National Assembly has two chambers, the Senate and the House of Representatives. Together they pass bills, approve budgets, and investigate waste.

steps.title: The executive carries out laws and runs daily government
steps.display: Section 5: President (Federation) and Governors (States) execute and maintain laws
working: Federal executive powers sit with the President, Vice-President, and Ministers (s. 5(1), s. 130, s. 147).
State executive powers sit with the Governor, Deputy Governor, and Commissioners (s. 5(2), s. 176).
steps.narration: Laws on paper do nothing until someone puts them to work. That is why we have the executive. Picture a compound head making sure everyone actually sweeps the yard on Saturday. The President leads this team for Nigeria, using ministers and civil servants to run schools, roads, and policing.

steps.title: The judiciary interprets laws and settles disputes
steps.display: Section 6: Courts decide disputes between persons and between government and citizens
working: Superior courts of record include the Supreme Court, Court of Appeal, Federal High Court, National Industrial Court, and State High Courts (s. 6(5)).
Judicial powers cover disputes between citizens and government (s. 6(6)(b)); lawmakers cannot oust court jurisdiction (s. 4(8)).
steps.narration: What happens when a citizen says the government broke its own rule? You need a neutral referee, like an umpire in a football match. The judiciary plays that role. Courts listen to both sides, explain what the law means, and can cancel unlawful government acts. Keep that in mind.

steps.title: Separation of powers keeps personnel and functions distinct
steps.display: Sections 4, 5, 6 and 147(4): Separate branches, and a legislator appointed Minister vacates the seat
working: Under s. 68(1)(d) and s. 147(4), a National Assembly member who takes the oath as Minister resigns from the legislature.
Under s. 109(1)(d), a State Assembly member who becomes a Commissioner or Minister vacates the seat.
steps.narration: Why not let the same person sit in parliament and also serve as a minister? Because judging your own work is never honest. Suppose a class rep marks their own homework. Nigeria forbids that mix. If a lawmaker becomes a federal minister, they must leave their parliamentary seat immediately.

steps.title: Checks and balances let each arm restrain the others
steps.display: Veto override (s. 58)  |  Confirmation & impeachment (ss. 143, 147)  |  Judicial review (ss. 1(3), 4(8))
working: Executive checks legislature: President has 30 days to assent or withhold assent to a bill (s. 58(4)).
Legislature checks executive: two-thirds of each House overrides a veto (s. 58(5)); Senate confirms Ministers (s. 147(2)); National Assembly can remove the President for gross misconduct (s. 143).

Judiciary checks both: courts void laws inconsistent with the Constitution (ss. 1(3), 4(8)). Executive and Senate check judiciary through NJC-recommended appointments and s. 292 removals (ss. 231, 292).
steps.narration: Separation alone is not enough if one branch runs wild. Think of three market union officers who each hold one key to the cash box. The President can refuse a bill. Parliament can override that refusal with two-thirds support. See how the court can stop both? That mutual watch is checks and balances.

steps.title: Read the worked problem and check what the Constitution says
steps.display: Question: Under the 1999 Constitution, if the President withholds assent to an ordinary bill, how can it still become law?
working: Options: (A) By a simple majority vote of the Senate alone
(B) By passing the bill again with a two-thirds majority of each House of the National Assembly
(C) By getting the Chief Justice of Nigeria to sign the bill
(D) By submitting the bill to a national referendum
steps.narration: Let us work through a classic question together. Imagine the President refuses to sign a bill into law. How can lawmakers push it through? Before guessing, recall why checks and balances exist. We must not let parliament bypass the President too easily, so a tiny vote will not work.

steps.title: Eliminate the wrong options one by one
steps.display: Wrong: (A) one House and simple majority  |  (C) Chief Justice does not sign bills  |  (D) no referendum for ordinary bills
working: Rule out (A): both the Senate and House of Representatives must pass the bill, and simple majority is not enough to override.
Rule out (C): the judiciary interprets laws under s. 6; the Chief Justice has no power to assent to bills.
Rule out (D): referendums apply under s. 8 for creating States or local areas, not ordinary bill overrides.
Correct: (B) Section 58(5) requires each House to pass the bill again by a two-thirds majority.
steps.narration: Let us knock out the wrong choices one by one. A fails because one chamber with a simple vote is too weak. C fails because judges interpret laws, they never sign bills. D fails because referendums are for creating states. That leaves B, a two-thirds vote in both chambers.

steps.title: Practice question on checks over judicial and ministerial acts
steps.display: Practice question: Which pair of powers shows the legislature checking the executive under the 1999 Constitution?
working: Options: (A) Appointing State Governors and dissolving Local Government Councils
(B) Confirming Ministerial nominees and investigating how appropriated funds are spent
(C) Signing bills into law and commanding the Armed Forces
(D) Issuing writs of habeas corpus and declaring statutes void
steps.narration: Now try a practice question in the exact JAMB style. Notice what it asks for. We want powers where the lawmaking arm watches over the executive arm. Watch closely as you scan each pair. Many students get tricked because every option names real government jobs, just attached to the wrong branch.

steps.title: Test each option against sections 5, 6, 58, 88 and 147
steps.display: Right: (B) Senate confirmation (s. 147(2)) and legislative investigation (s. 88)
working: (A) Wrong: Governors are elected (s. 178), not appointed by lawmakers.
(B) Right: Senate confirms Ministers (s. 147(2)) and National Assembly investigates fund spending (s. 88).
(C) Wrong: assenting to bills (s. 58) and commanding the Armed Forces (s. 218) belong to the President.
(D) Wrong: issuing writs and voiding unlawful statutes belong to the courts (ss. 4(8), 6, 46).
steps.narration: Check each pair carefully. Option A is wrong because voters elect Governors. Option C lists powers of the President, not parliament. Option D belongs to judges in court. Only B gives two real legislative checks, approving ministerial nominees and investigating how public money was spent. Notice how knowing each branch stops careless mistakes.

steps.title: Do not confuse impeachment steps with court trials
steps.display: Wrong: Supreme Court removes the President  |  Right: National Assembly + CJN 7-person panel (s. 143)
working: Under s. 143, notice requires \frac{1}{3} of National Assembly members; investigation motion needs \frac{2}{3} of each House.
CJN appoints a 7-person panel; if proved, \frac{2}{3} of each House removes the President, and s. 143(10) bars court review.
steps.narration: Here is a huge exam trap. Students often think the Supreme Court removes a President during impeachment. Not true! In Nigeria, lawmakers start and finish impeachment with two-thirds votes. The Chief Justice only picks the seven-person panel to investigate. Even better, courts cannot question the lawmakers' final decision.

steps.title: Separation of powers does not mean zero overlap
steps.display: Wrong: Branches never touch each other  |  Right: Separate powers with constitutional checks
working: President signs bills (legislative role, s. 58); Senate confirms Ministers and Judges (executive and judicial checks, ss. 147, 231).
In a presidential system like Nigeria, overlap exists through checks, while dual membership in legislature and cabinet is barred (s. 147(4)).
steps.narration: Another trap is thinking separation means the three branches never talk. They interact constantly! The President signs laws, the Senate vets judges, and courts review statutes. What Nigeria forbids is one person holding two jobs across branches, like being a Senator and a Minister together.

steps.title: Three separate arms watching one another under the Constitution
steps.display: Legislature makes law (s. 4)  |  Executive applies law (s. 5)  |  Judiciary judges law (s. 6)
working: No branch stands alone: veto overrides, Senate confirmations, investigations, and judicial review keep power balanced.
steps.narration: Keep this one picture in your head. Government splits into law-makers, law-doers, and law-judges so tyranny cannot grow. Each arm has special constitutional tools to block abuse by the others. Know who does what, and these exam questions become easy marks.

quickCheck.stem: Practice: Under section 147(4) of the 1999 Constitution, what happens when a sitting member of the National Assembly takes the oath of office as a Federal Minister?

options.text: The member keeps both posts to link the cabinet and parliament
options.why: Wrong: holding both posts happens in a parliamentary system, whereas section 147(4) forbids dual membership in Nigeria's presidential system.

options.text: The member is deemed to have resigned from the National Assembly
options.why: Correct: under section 147(4) (and section 68(1)(d)), taking the oath as Minister automatically ends the member's legislative seat to preserve separation of powers.

options.text: The member is suspended without pay until the ministerial term ends
options.why: Wrong: the seat is vacated permanently upon taking the ministerial oath, not held in suspension.

options.text: The Senate President decides whether the member may keep the seat
options.why: Wrong: the Constitution makes resignation automatic under section 147(4), leaving no discretion to the Senate President.

steps.title: The rulebook every player must obey
steps.display: Constitution = supreme rulebook  |  Even the referee and captain must obey it
working: A constitution sits above every leader and every ordinary law.
Any rule that clashes with it is thrown out.
steps.narration: Think of a village football tournament. Before kickoff, everyone agrees on one rulebook. Even the team captain and referee must obey it, or the match falls apart.

steps.title: Constitutional supremacy makes the Constitution the highest law
steps.display: Section 1(1)–(3): Constitution binds all authorities and persons; any inconsistent law is void
working: Section 1(1): supreme and binding across Nigeria.
Section 1(2): nobody may take control of government except as the Constitution provides.
Section 1(3): any law inconsistent with the Constitution is void to the extent of the inconsistency.
steps.narration: Why do we need a highest rulebook? Because without one, leaders could rewrite rules whenever they wish. Suppose a market chairman tries to ban elections after winning once. Under section one, any law or order that fights the Constitution is immediately cancelled by the courts.

steps.title: Four syllabus types: written, unwritten, rigid and flexible
steps.display: JAMB Syllabus classification: Form (Written vs Unwritten)  |  Amendment process (Rigid vs Flexible)
working: Written vs unwritten groups constitutions by whether their fundamental rules sit in a single codified document.
Rigid vs flexible groups constitutions by whether changing them requires a special, harder procedure than passing ordinary laws.
steps.narration: Exam questions sort constitutions in two ways. First, is it written in one single book, or spread across unwritten customs and old laws? Second, how hard is it to change? Picture a school rulebook locked in a safe versus one written on a chalkboard. We compare those two ideas next.

steps.title: Nigeria's 1999 Constitution is written and organised in one document
steps.display: 1999 Constitution: Preamble + Chapters I–VIII + Seven Schedules
working: Codified into one official text covering general provisions, rights, citizenship, legislature, executive, judiciary, and schedules.
Gives citizens and courts one clear reference text to test whether laws obey section 1(3).
steps.narration: Let us look at Nigeria's own rulebook. It is written, meaning you can pick up one bound document and point to the exact page. Say a police officer stops a peaceful meeting. A lawyer can open Chapter Four, section forty, and show the judge the exact words in black and white.

steps.title: Nigeria's Constitution is rigid under section 9
steps.display: Ordinary bill: simple majority (ss. 56, 58)  |  Constitution alteration: \frac{2}{3} or \frac{4}{5} + \frac{2}{3} States (s. 9)
working: General alteration (s. 9(2)): \frac{2}{3} of all members of each House of the National Assembly AND approval by \frac{2}{3} of all State Houses of Assembly.
Entrenched parts — s. 8 (state creation), s. 9, and Chapter IV (rights) — require \frac{4}{5} of all members of each House AND \frac{2}{3} of all State Houses (s. 9(3)).
steps.narration: Notice how hard it is to edit Nigeria's Constitution! An ordinary law only needs a simple majority of members present. Changing the Constitution needs two-thirds of every member in both federal chambers, plus two-thirds of all state assemblies. Protecting human rights is even tougher, needing four-fifths! That special hurdle makes it rigid.

steps.title: Read a question on amending fundamental rights
steps.display: Question: Which vote is required under section 9(3) to alter a Fundamental Right in Chapter IV of the 1999 Constitution?
working: Options: (A) Simple majority of members present and voting in each House
(B) Two-thirds majority of all members of each House and two-thirds of all State Houses of Assembly
(C) Four-fifths majority of all members of each House and approval by two-thirds of all State Houses of Assembly
(D) Executive order signed by the President and approved by the Supreme Court
steps.narration: Let us tackle a worked question on rigidity. We want to change a right in Chapter Four. Why should that be harder than passing a normal road-repair bill? Because rights protect every citizen from sudden majority moods. Keep that clue in mind as we eliminate the wrong choices.

steps.title: Eliminate the wrong thresholds one by one
steps.display: Wrong: (A) ordinary law vote  |  (B) general s. 9(2) rule  |  (D) President and Court cannot amend
working: Rule out (A): simple majority under s. 56(2) passes ordinary bills, not constitutional amendments.
Rule out (B): \frac{2}{3} of each House plus \frac{2}{3} of States applies to ordinary provisions under s. 9(2), not s. 8, s. 9, or Chapter IV.
Rule out (D): neither the President alone nor the Supreme Court can alter the Constitution; s. 9 vests alteration in the legislatures.
Correct: (C) Section 9(3) demands \frac{4}{5} of all members of each House plus resolution of \frac{2}{3} of all State Houses of Assembly.
steps.narration: Now knock them out cleanly. Option A is for ordinary bills, not the Constitution. Option B is the famous trap! Two-thirds works for most sections, not Chapter Four, section eight, or section nine. Option D gives amendment power to the wrong arms. So C is the exact answer.

steps.title: Practice question on constitutional supremacy
steps.display: Practice question: A State House of Assembly passes a Law that violates section 1(3) by conflicting with the 1999 Constitution. What is the legal effect?
working: Options: (A) The State Law applies inside that State until the Governor repeals it
(B) Both laws apply side by side unless the Senate intervenes
(C) The State Law is void to the extent of its inconsistency with the Constitution
(D) The Constitution is automatically amended to match the State Law
steps.narration: Here is a JAMB-style practice question. Notice the core issue. A state law clashes directly with the Constitution. Remember who sits at the very top of Nigeria's legal ladder. Let us test each option against section one of the 1999 Constitution to see which one holds up.

steps.title: Apply section 1(3) to pick the right option
steps.display: Right: (C) Constitution prevails; conflicting State Law is void to the extent of inconsistency (s. 1(3))
working: (A) Wrong: no State Law can override the supreme Constitution inside a State (s. 1(1), (3)).
(B) Wrong: conflicting rules cannot both be valid; the Constitution prevails.
(C) Right: section 1(3) declares any inconsistent law void to the extent of the inconsistency.
(D) Wrong: only the special procedure in section 9 can alter the Constitution.
steps.narration: Check each option against section one. Option A fails because the Constitution binds every state without exception. Option B fails because two clashing laws cannot both stand. Option D flips the hierarchy upside down. Only C matches section one subsection three, making the conflicting part completely void.

steps.title: Do not mix up s. 9(2) and s. 9(3) amendment fractions
steps.display: General clauses: \frac{2}{3} National Assembly + \frac{2}{3} States  |  ss. 8, 9 & Ch. IV: \frac{4}{5} National Assembly + \frac{2}{3} States
working: And under s. 9(4), \frac{2}{3} or \frac{4}{5} is counted out of ALL members in ss. 48–49, not just those present that day!
steps.narration: Watch this double trap in section nine! First, most sections need two-thirds, while state creation, section nine, and human rights need four-fifths in the National Assembly. Second, count all members, even empty seats! Skipping absent lawmakers is how many candidates pick the wrong fraction.

steps.title: Written does not always mean rigid, nor unwritten flexible
steps.display: Form (Written vs Unwritten)  ≠  Amendment difficulty (Rigid vs Flexible)
working: Form asks whether rules sit in a single codified text; rigidity asks whether amendment needs a special procedure above ordinary law-making.
Nigeria's 1999 Constitution is both written (one document) and rigid (special s. 9 supermajorities).
steps.narration: Students often treat written and rigid as the same word. They answer two different questions! Written asks how the rules are packaged. Rigid asks how hard they are to change. Nigeria happens to be both written and rigid, because section nine blocks easy changes.

steps.title: Supremacy plus a rigid amendment rule protects the Constitution
steps.display: Section 1: Supreme over all laws  |  Section 9: Supermajorities required to alter
working: Nigeria's 1999 Constitution is written and rigid, sitting above every federal and state law.
steps.narration: Here is the core idea to carry into your exam. A constitution is not an ordinary law. In Nigeria, it is written in one supreme book, and section nine locks it with tough supermajorities. Remember those two rules, and constitution questions will never catch you out.

quickCheck.stem: Practice: Under section 9(4) of the 1999 Constitution, how is the two-thirds or four-fifths majority in the Senate and House of Representatives calculated for a constitutional alteration?

options.text: As a fraction of only the members present and voting on that day
options.why: Wrong: ordinary legislative votes use members present and voting (s. 56(1)), whereas section 9(4) requires the fraction of ALL members regardless of vacancies.

options.text: As a fraction of the total membership specified in sections 48 and 49, notwithstanding any vacancy
options.why: Correct: section 9(4) states that the required two-thirds or four-fifths is calculated against the full constitutional membership (ss. 48–49), ignoring vacancies.

options.text: As a fraction of members who belong to the ruling political party
options.why: Wrong: party membership plays no role in calculating constitutional amendment thresholds under section 9.

options.text: As a simple majority in a joint sitting of both Houses
options.why: Wrong: each House votes separately by two-thirds or four-fifths majority under section 9(2) and (3), not by simple majority.

lessons.title: Rule of law and fundamental human rights

steps.title: No one is above the traffic light
steps.display: Red light stops everyone: rich car, okada rider, and uniform officer alike
working: The law rules the country, not the personal wishes of whoever holds power.
Every citizen carries protected rights that the courts can defend.
steps.narration: At a busy junction, the red light stops the big man's jeep and the okada rider alike. Under the rule of law, no leader sits above the law.

steps.title: Rule of law: supremacy of law, equality and independent courts
steps.display: Sections 1(1), 4(8), 6(6)(b), 17(2)(a) and (e): Everyone equal before independent courts
working: Supremacy of law: Constitution binds all authorities and persons (s. 1(1)); laws cannot block court access (s. 4(8)).
Equality before the law: every citizen has equal rights, obligations, and opportunities before the law (s. 17(2)(a)).
Independent courts: judges are impartial and citizens can sue government authorities (ss. 6(6)(b), 17(2)(e)).
steps.narration: Why does the rule of law matter? Because power without rules turns into fear. Imagine a local chief who jails anyone he dislikes without a hearing. Nigeria blocks that through three pillars. Law sits above leaders, every citizen faces the same law, and independent courts settle disputes fairly.

steps.title: Chapter IV protects life, dignity, personal liberty and fair hearing
steps.display: Sections 33–36: Life, no torture, arrest safeguards (24 hrs notice; 1–2 days to court), fair hearing
working: Life (s. 33) and dignity — no torture, slavery, or forced labour (s. 34).

Personal liberty (s. 35): right to stay silent (s. 35(2)), written arrest reasons within 24 hours (s. 35(3)), and court appearance within 1 day if a court is within 40 km, or 2 days otherwise (s. 35(5)).
Fair hearing (s. 36): public trial within reasonable time, presumed innocent until proved guilty (s. 36(5)), no retroactive crime (s. 36(8)).
steps.narration: Let us see how those protections work on the street. Suppose police arrest a trader at a market. Under section thirty-five, she has the right to stay silent until she sees a lawyer. She must get written reasons within twenty-four hours and see a court within one or two days.

steps.title: Chapter IV protects civic freedoms, equality and property
steps.display: Sections 37–44: Privacy, religion, speech, assembly, movement, non-discrimination and property
working: Privacy (s. 37), thought and religion (s. 38), expression and press (s. 39), peaceful assembly and association (s. 40).
Movement throughout Nigeria (s. 41), freedom from discrimination by origin, sex, religion, or opinion (s. 42), and property rights with prompt compensation on compulsory takeover (ss. 43–44).
steps.narration: Freedom is not just about avoiding jail. You also need room to speak, worship, travel, and earn a living. Think of a young graduate moving from Kano to Lagos to open a shop. Sections forty-one and forty-two protect her right to live anywhere in Nigeria without ethnic discrimination.

steps.title: Rights have legal limits and can be enforced in the High Court
steps.display: Section 45: Democratic limits and emergencies  |  Section 46: High Court redress and legal aid
working: Section 45(1): rights in ss. 37–41 may be limited by laws reasonably justifiable for defence, public safety, public order, morality, health, or others' rights.
Section 45(2): during a s. 305 state of emergency, limited measures may affect ss. 33 (war only) or 35, never s. 36(8).
Section 46(1)–(4): anyone whose Chapter IV right is infringed may apply directly to a State or Federal High Court; National Assembly provides legal aid for indigent citizens.
steps.narration: Are human rights unlimited? No! Your freedom to swing your fist ends where your neighbour's nose begins. For example, during a deadly epidemic, the government can restrict large gatherings to save lives under section forty-five. And if officials abuse your rights, you can ask a High Court for protection.

steps.title: Read a question on lawful arrest time limits
steps.display: Question: Police arrest a citizen for theft in a city with a Magistrate's Court 5 km away. Under section 35(5), what is a 'reasonable time' to bring her to court?
working: Options: (A) Within 1 day (24 hours)
(B) Within 7 days
(C) Within 14 days
(D) Within 2 months
steps.narration: Let us work through a practical rights question. Remember why section thirty-five gives strict clocks. If police could hold suspects forever without seeing a judge, liberty would be a joke. Check the distance given here. Five kilometres is well inside forty kilometres. Keep that distance rule in mind.

steps.title: Check the Constitution's clock and rule out wrong options
steps.display: Wrong: (B) 7 days, (C) 14 days, (D) 2 months (trial limit under s. 35(4)(a), not first court appearance)
working: Rule out (B) and (C): section 35(5) never sets 7-day or 14-day pre-arraignment windows.
Rule out (D): 2 months in s. 35(4)(a) is the maximum wait for trial when held without bail after arrest, not the first appearance before a court.
Correct: (A) Under s. 35(5)(a), when a competent court is within a 40 km radius, 'a reasonable time' means 1 day.
steps.narration: Watch how the distractors try to trick you. Options B and C are pure guesses with no constitutional basis. Option D is clever because two months appears in section thirty-five, yet that is for starting trial without bail, not first seeing a magistrate. Within forty kilometres means one day, option A.

steps.title: Practice question on enforcing fundamental rights versus Chapter II
steps.display: Practice question: Which right or objective in the 1999 Constitution can a citizen directly enforce in a High Court under section 46?
working: Options: (A) Free university education under section 18 (Chapter II)
(B) Adequate medical and health facilities under section 17(3)(d) (Chapter II)
(C) Freedom from discrimination under section 42 (Chapter IV)
(D) Protection of the environment under section 20 (Chapter II)
steps.narration: Here is a practice question on a favourite exam distinction. Not every good promise in the Constitution works the same way in court. Check which Chapter each option comes from. Remember, section forty-six only unlocks the High Court for one specific Chapter. Let us test all four.

steps.title: Distinguish non-justiciable Chapter II from enforceable Chapter IV
steps.display: Right: (C) Section 42 is in Chapter IV (enforceable under s. 46); (A), (B) and (D) are in Chapter II (barred by s. 6(6)(c))
working: (A), (B), (D) Wrong: sections 17, 18, and 20 sit in Chapter II; section 6(6)(c) bars courts from deciding whether laws or government conform to Chapter II.
(C) Right: section 42 sits in Chapter IV (Fundamental Rights), directly enforceable in a High Court under section 46.
steps.narration: Look how clean that rule is! Education, health care, and environment sit in Chapter Two, which section six subsection six c says courts cannot enforce directly. Freedom from discrimination sits in Chapter Four. That makes C the only right a citizen can carry straight to the High Court under section forty-six.

steps.title: Do not mistake Chapter II goals for enforceable Chapter IV rights
steps.display: Chapter II (ss. 13–24): Directive Principles (s. 6(6)(c) non-justiciable)  |  Chapter IV (ss. 33–46): Enforceable Rights
working: Courts cannot enforce Chapter II promises directly unless turned into law by the legislature (s. 6(6)(c)).
Chapter IV rights are directly justiciable in a High Court (s. 46).
steps.narration: Many students see 'right' ideas like free education or jobs and assume they can sue government in court tomorrow. Careful! Those sit in Chapter Two as guiding goals, not Chapter Four rights. Under section six subsection six c, courts can only enforce Chapter Four directly.

steps.title: Even during a state of emergency, some rights cannot be stripped
steps.display: Section 45(2) proviso: No retroactive crimes (s. 36(8)), and no killing except lawful acts of war
working: Emergency derogations under s. 45(2) only cover s. 33 (war deaths) and s. 35, and only as reasonably justifiable.
Fair hearing protection against backdated criminal laws (s. 36(8)) can never be suspended.
steps.narration: Do not think a state of emergency wipes out all human rights. Look at the proviso in section forty-five. Even in an emergency, government cannot make an act a crime after you already did it. And any limit on liberty must still be reasonable for handling that emergency.

steps.title: The rule of law protects equal rights through independent courts
steps.display: Supremacy of Constitution (s. 1) + Chapter IV Rights (ss. 33–46) + High Court Access (s. 46)
working: Laws bind leaders and citizens alike; Chapter IV rights have narrow democratic limits and High Court protection.
steps.narration: Take away this one thread. The rule of law puts the Constitution above every leader. It treats every person equally. It also backs Chapter Four rights with independent courts. Know the arrest clocks, the Chapter Two split, and section forty-five limits.

quickCheck.stem: Practice: Under section 45(1) of the 1999 Constitution, which condition allows a law to validly restrict freedoms such as movement (s. 41) or assembly (s. 40)?

options.text: The President issues a personal directive without any Act or Law
options.why: Wrong: section 45(1) protects only a 'law that is reasonably justifiable in a democratic society', not arbitrary executive orders.

options.text: The law is reasonably justifiable in a democratic society for public safety, public order, defence, health, morality or protecting others' rights
options.why: Correct: section 45(1)(a)–(b) permits restrictions on ss. 37–41 only through laws reasonably justifiable in a democratic society for those listed public interests.

options.text: The restriction targets only citizens from particular ethnic groups
options.why: Wrong: targeting people by ethnic group violates section 42's ban on discrimination.

options.text: The law permanently abolishes High Court jurisdiction under section 46
options.why: Wrong: section 4(8) and section 46 preserve court access and forbid laws that oust court jurisdiction.

steps.title: Full member of the family compound
steps.display: Citizen = legal member of Nigeria  |  Enjoys rights and owes duties in return
working: You can belong by blood and birth, by marriage or family tie, or by earning full membership after years of living here.
steps.narration: Think of being a full member of a family compound. Everyone protects your place there. In return, you help keep the compound clean and safe.

steps.title: Citizenship by birth depends on Nigerian parentage or indigenous community
steps.display: Section 25: Born in Nigeria before 1 Oct 1960 (indigenous parent or grandparent), or after 1960 (citizen parent or grandparent), or abroad (citizen parent)
working: Born in Nigeria before independence (1 Oct 1960): parent or grandparent belonged to a community indigenous to Nigeria, AND at least one parent or grandparent was born in Nigeria (s. 25(1)(a)).
Born in Nigeria after 1 Oct 1960: either parent or any grandparent is a Nigerian citizen (s. 25(1)(b)).
Born outside Nigeria: either parent is a Nigerian citizen (s. 25(1)(c)).
steps.narration: Does simply being born inside a Nigerian hospital make a baby a citizen? Not by itself! Nigeria uses blood ties, not just soil. Suppose two foreign tourists have a baby in Abuja today. That baby is not a citizen by birth unless a parent or grandparent is Nigerian.

steps.title: Citizenship by registration and citizenship by naturalisation
steps.display: Section 26: Registration (married woman or grandchild)  |  Section 27: Naturalisation (15 years residence + local acceptance)
working: Registration (s. 26): good character, intent to reside, Oath of Allegiance — open to (a) any woman married to a Nigerian citizen, or (b) adult born abroad with a Nigerian grandparent.

Naturalisation (s. 27): full age, good character, intent to reside, Governor's attestation of local acceptance and assimilation, useful contribution, Oath of Allegiance, plus 15 continuous years residence (or 12 months + 15 years out of 20).
steps.narration: What if someone has no Nigerian parent, yet wants to belong? There are two legal doors. A foreign woman who marries a Nigerian man can apply by registration under section twenty-six. A foreign engineer who lives peacefully in Enugu for fifteen continuous years can apply for naturalisation under section twenty-seven.

steps.title: Dual citizenship, renunciation and deprivation rules
steps.display: Section 28: Birth citizens keep dual nationality; registered or naturalised cannot  |  Sections 29–30: Renunciation & deprivation
working: Dual citizenship (s. 28): a citizen by birth does NOT forfeit Nigerian citizenship by holding another passport; a registered or naturalised citizen must renounce any non-birth foreign citizenship within 12 months.
Renunciation (s. 29): adult citizen may declare renunciation; President may withhold registration during war or if against public policy.

Deprivation (s. 30): President may deprive a naturalised citizen (imprisonment ≥ 3 yrs within 7 yrs) or registered or naturalised citizen (disloyalty or trading with enemy); a citizen by birth CANNOT be deprived.
steps.narration: Here is where students often slip up. Can a Nigerian hold two passports? Yes, if you are a citizen by birth! For example, a child of Nigerian parents born in London keeps both. But someone who naturalised must give up their old non-birth nationality within twelve months. And birth citizens can never be stripped of citizenship.

steps.title: Duties of citizens and obligations of the State
steps.display: Section 24: Citizen duties (obey Constitution, pay tax, assist law)  |  Section 14(2)(b): State's primary purpose is security and welfare
working: Section 24 duties: abide by Constitution, respect Flag, Anthem and Pledge, defend Nigeria, respect others' dignity, aid community, assist lawful agencies, declare income honestly and pay tax promptly.
State obligations (ss. 13–22, 14(2)(b), 33–46): protect fundamental rights, ensure security and welfare of the people, and uphold freedom, equality, and justice.
steps.narration: Citizenship is a two-way street. Why should the State protect your home and rights while you give nothing back? Suppose everyone refused to pay tax or obey traffic rules. Roads and schools would collapse. Section twenty-four lists your duties, like paying tax promptly, while section fourteen tasks government with your security and welfare.

steps.title: Read a worked question on citizenship by birth
steps.display: Question: Kofi's parents are both Ghanaian citizens. Kofi was born in Lagos in 2005 and has lived there all his life. Under section 25, what is Kofi's citizenship status?
working: Options: (A) Citizen of Nigeria by birth
(B) Citizen of Nigeria by registration automatically at age 18
(C) Not a Nigerian citizen by birth; he must apply for naturalisation under section 27 if qualified
(D) Dual citizen of Nigeria and Ghana automatically
steps.narration: Let us test section twenty-five with a realistic case. A boy named Kofi grew up in Lagos after arriving at birth in two thousand and five. Both his parents hold Ghanaian citizenship. Remember our rule on blood versus soil! Do not get fooled by where he grew up. Check each option.

steps.title: Rule out the wrong options using sections 25, 26 and 27
steps.display: Wrong: (A) no Nigerian parent or grandparent  |  (B) registration is not automatic  |  (D) not a birth citizen
working: Rule out (A): section 25(1)(b) requires at least one parent or grandparent to be a Nigerian citizen for anyone born in Nigeria after 1 Oct 1960.
Rule out (B): section 26 registration applies only to a woman married to a Nigerian or a grandchild of a citizen born abroad, and requires application.
Rule out (D): Kofi does not acquire Nigerian citizenship at birth, so he has no automatic Nigerian dual citizenship.
Correct: (C) With 15 years continuous residence and meeting s. 27 conditions, Kofi may apply for naturalisation.
steps.narration: Watch how each wrong option breaks down. Option A fails because post-independence birth in Nigeria needs a Nigerian parent or grandparent. Option B fails because registration is neither automatic nor for Kofi's situation. Option D fails for the same reason. That leaves C, applying to naturalise after fifteen years.

steps.title: Practice question on deprivation and dual citizenship
steps.display: Practice question: Which Nigerian citizen may be deprived of Nigerian citizenship by the President under section 30?
working: Options: (A) A citizen by birth convicted of an offence abroad
(B) A citizen by birth who acquires Canadian citizenship
(C) A citizen by naturalisation sentenced to 4 years in prison within 5 years of naturalising
(D) A citizen by birth who publicly criticises government economic policy
steps.narration: Now try a practice question on losing citizenship. This tests sections twenty-eight and thirty together. Ask yourself who the President has power to strip of citizenship, and who is completely protected. Look at how each option names either birth citizenship or naturalisation. Spot the difference right away.

steps.title: Apply section 28 and section 30 to pick the answer
steps.display: Right: (C) Section 30(1) allows deprivation if a naturalised citizen is jailed ≥ 3 years within 7 years
working: (A) Wrong: section 30 explicitly excludes any 'citizen of Nigeria by birth' from deprivation.
(B) Wrong: section 28 allows a citizen by birth to hold dual citizenship.
(C) Right: section 30(1) empowers the President to deprive a naturalised citizen sentenced to at least 3 years imprisonment within 7 years of naturalisation.
(D) Wrong: birth citizens cannot be deprived, and peaceful criticism falls under freedom of expression (s. 39).
steps.narration: Three options fall at once! Why? Each one names a citizen by birth. Section thirty protects birth citizens from ever losing citizenship. Section twenty-eight also protects their dual nationality. Option C describes a naturalised citizen jailed for four years within five years. That matches section thirty.

steps.title: Being born in Nigeria after 1960 alone does not grant citizenship
steps.display: Wrong: Born in Nigeria = citizen  |  Right: Post-1960 birth needs citizen parent or grandparent (s. 25(1)(b))
working: Before 1 Oct 1960: parent or grandparent from an indigenous community plus birth in Nigeria of a parent or grandparent.
After 1 Oct 1960: birth in Nigeria PLUS a Nigerian citizen parent or grandparent.
steps.narration: This trap catches thousands of students! They hear 'citizenship by birth' and assume anyone born on Nigerian soil qualifies. Not here. After independence in nineteen sixty, a child born in Nigeria still needs at least one Nigerian parent or grandparent. Soil without blood is not enough.

steps.title: Only citizens by birth have unrestricted dual citizenship
steps.display: Birth citizen: Dual citizenship allowed  |  Registered or Naturalised: Must renounce prior non-birth citizenship within 12 months
working: Section 28(1) forfeits citizenship if a non-birth citizen acquires or keeps citizenship of a country where they are not a citizen by birth.
Also remember s. 131(a) and s. 177(a): only a citizen by birth can run for President or Governor!
steps.narration: Do not assume every Nigerian citizen shares the exact same rules on dual nationality or top offices. A naturalised citizen must drop their previous non-birth passport within twelve months under section twenty-eight. Also notice sections one-thirty-one and one-seventy-seven. Top executive offices require birth citizenship.

steps.title: Three legal doors in, strong birth protections, and mutual duties
steps.display: Birth (s. 25)  |  Registration (s. 26)  |  Naturalisation (s. 27)  |  Duties (s. 24)
working: Birth citizenship requires Nigerian parentage or ancestry and cannot be taken away; every citizen owes duties under s. 24.
steps.narration: Keep these three doors clear. Birth comes through Nigerian parents or grandparents and can never be taken away. Registration fits foreign wives and overseas grandchildren. Naturalisation takes fifteen years of residence. Together, rights and duties bind citizens and the State into one community.

quickCheck.stem: Practice: Under section 27(2) of the 1999 Constitution, which residence period qualifies a foreign national to apply for citizenship by naturalisation?

options.text: Continuous residence in Nigeria for 5 years immediately before applying
options.why: Wrong: 5 years is far short of the constitutional 15-year requirement in section 27(2)(g).

options.text: Continuous residence for 15 years, or 12 continuous months plus 15 years total in the preceding 20 years
options.why: Correct: section 27(2)(g)(i)–(ii) requires either 15 continuous years or 12 continuous months plus an aggregate of 15 years within the preceding 20 years.

options.text: Marriage to a Nigerian citizen for 2 years
options.why: Wrong: marriage of a foreign woman to a Nigerian citizen leads to citizenship by registration under section 26, not naturalisation under section 27.

options.text: Ownership of land in any Nigerian State for 10 years
options.why: Wrong: owning property does not replace the 15-year residency and Governor's community-acceptance requirements in section 27(2).

lessons.title: The electoral process, franchise and electoral bodies

steps.title: Choosing the class captain with a neutral referee
steps.display: Voters pick leaders (franchise)  |  Neutral referee (INEC or SIEC) counts and declares results
working: Every qualified adult gets one vote.
An independent umpire runs the election so candidates cannot count their own votes.
steps.narration: When a class picks its captain, every pupil gets one secret vote. The teacher counts the slips. Elections work similarly, with neutral commissions acting as referees.

steps.title: Franchise in Nigeria is universal adult suffrage at age 18
steps.display: Sections 77(2), 117(2), 132(5), 178(5): Every Nigerian citizen aged 18+ residing in Nigeria may register to vote
working: Direct elections for Senate, House of Representatives, State House of Assembly, President, and Governor.
Same voter eligibility applies to Local Government Council elections under s. 7(4).
steps.narration: Franchise simply means the legal right to vote. Picture a young woman turning eighteen in Kano. She can now visit a registration centre for her voter's card. Nigeria uses universal adult suffrage from eighteen years. Wealth, sex, or tribe never blocks a registered adult.

steps.title: Candidate age and qualification rules after the Fourth Alteration
steps.display: Age limits: House of Reps & State Assembly = 25  |  Senate, Governor & President = 35
working: Fourth Alteration No. 27 (2017) lowered President from 40 to 35 (s. 131(b)), House of Reps from 30 to 25 (s. 65(1)(b)), and State Assembly from 30 to 25 (s. 106(b)); Senate and Governor remain 35 (ss. 65(1)(a), 177(b)).
All require Nigerian citizenship (by birth for President and Governor), School Certificate or equivalent, and political party sponsorship.
steps.narration: Voting is one side; running for office is the other. Notice how the Fourth Alteration opened doors for younger candidates! For instance, a twenty-six-year-old teacher can now contest for the House of Representatives or a State Assembly. For Senate, Governor, or President, you must be thirty-five.

steps.title: Presidential and governorship winners need both votes and spread
steps.display: Sections 134 & 179: Highest votes + at least 25% (\frac{1}{4}) in \frac{2}{3} of States and FCT (or \frac{2}{3} of LGAs)
working: President (s. 134): highest votes cast AND ≥ \frac{1}{4} of votes in each of at least \frac{2}{3} of all 36 States and the FCT.
Governor (s. 179): highest votes cast AND ≥ \frac{1}{4} of votes in each of at least \frac{2}{3} of all Local Government Areas in the State; otherwise a run-off follows within 21 days.
steps.narration: Why can't a candidate win the presidency by sweeping just three huge cities? Because Nigeria wants a leader with support across the whole country. Suppose one candidate wins huge numbers in one region yet gets almost nothing elsewhere. Without one-quarter in two-thirds of states, a run-off is called.

steps.title: INEC runs federal and state elections; SIEC runs local council elections
steps.display: INEC (s. 153, 3rd Sched. Pt. I Item F)  |  SIEC (s. 197, 3rd Sched. Pt. II Item B)  |  Tribunals (ss. 239, 285)
working: INEC (Chairman ≥ 40 yrs + 12 National Commissioners ≥ 35 yrs + 1 REC per State and FCT) conducts Presidential, National Assembly, Governorship, and State Assembly elections, registers and monitors parties, and manages voter registration.
SIEC (Chairman + 5–7 members) conducts Local Government Council elections in each State.
Election petitions (s. 285): filed within 21 days; tribunal decides within 180 days; appeals within 60 days. Court of Appeal has original jurisdiction over Presidential petitions (s. 239).
steps.narration: Notice how election duties split between two commissions so neither does everything. Think of national football leagues versus state cup matches. INEC runs presidential, gubernatorial, and legislative elections, and registers parties. Each state has a SIEC to run local council elections. And tribunals settle disputes under strict clocks.

sources.where: ss. 153, 154, 158, 197, 239, 285; 3rd Sched. Pt. I Item F paras. 14–15, Pt. II Item B paras. 3–4

steps.title: Read a question on recalling an elected legislator
steps.display: Question: Voters in a Federal Constituency lose confidence in their Representative. Under section 69, what must happen for a recall to succeed?
working: Options: (A) The Governor writes to the Speaker to declare the seat vacant
(B) A petition signed by > \frac{1}{2} of registered voters is verified by INEC, then approved by a simple majority in a referendum within 90 days
(C) The political party withdraws the member's membership card
(D) Two-thirds of the House of Representatives votes to expel the member
steps.narration: Let us work through a recall question. Recall means voters taking back the job they gave a lawmaker before the term ends. Ask yourself who owns that seat. Not the Governor, and not even the party boss. Keep the voters and INEC at the centre as we test each option.

steps.title: Eliminate the wrong options using sections 68 and 69
steps.display: Wrong: (A) Governor has no recall role  |  (C) party withdrawal is not recall  |  (D) expulsion is not s. 69 recall
working: Rule out (A): the executive cannot remove an elected federal legislator.
Rule out (C): recall is a voter-driven constitutional process under s. 69, not internal party discipline.
Rule out (D): s. 69 vests recall in registered constituency voters, not fellow legislators.
Correct: (B) Petition signed by over half of registered constituency voters, verified by INEC, and approved by simple majority in a 90-day referendum (s. 69(a)–(b)).
steps.narration: Check each distractor. Option A puts a Governor over federal lawmakers, which breaks separation of powers. Option C confuses party quarrels with constitutional recall. Option D hands the power to other lawmakers instead of constituents. Only B matches section sixty-nine, starting with over half of registered voters.

steps.title: Practice question on minimum age qualifications
steps.display: Practice question: After the Fourth Alteration (No. 27) Act 2017, what is the minimum age to contest for the House of Representatives?
working: Options: (A) 18 years
(B) 25 years
(C) 30 years
(D) 35 years
steps.narration: Try this JAMB-style practice question. Notice how closely the four numbers sit next to each other. Eighteen, twenty-five, thirty, and thirty-five are all famous constitutional ages, which is why students mix them up. Recall which offices changed in two thousand and seventeen and which stayed at thirty-five.

steps.title: Match each age to its exact constitutional office
steps.display: Right: (B) 25 years (s. 65(1)(b), altered from 30 by 4th Alteration No. 27)
working: (A) Wrong: 18 years is the minimum voting age (s. 77(2)), not the age to run for the House of Representatives.
(B) Right: 4th Alteration No. 27 lowered the House of Representatives (s. 65(1)(b)) and State Assembly (s. 106(b)) minimum age from 30 to 25.
(C) Wrong: 30 years was the old pre-2017 age before the Fourth Alteration.
(D) Wrong: 35 years applies to the Senate (s. 65(1)(a)), Governor (s. 177(b)), and President (s. 131(b)).
steps.narration: Pin each number to its true job. Eighteen lets you register to vote. Thirty was the old House of Representatives rule before the amendment changed it. Thirty-five is for the Senate, Governors, and the President. That leaves twenty-five, option B, for both the House and State Assemblies.

steps.title: Do not assume the Fourth Alteration lowered Senate or Governor age to 30
steps.display: Lowered: President (40 → 35), House of Reps (30 → 25), State Assembly (30 → 25)  |  Unchanged: Senate (35), Governor (35)
working: Sections 65(1)(a) and 177(b) kept 35 years for the Senate and State Governor.
steps.narration: Here is a sneaky exam trap! Because people call the two thousand seventeen law 'Not Too Young To Run', students think every office dropped. President dropped to thirty-five, and lower houses dropped to twenty-five. Yet Senate and Governor stayed right at thirty-five! Always check which chamber the question names.

steps.title: Separate INEC's elections from SIEC's elections and know the petition court
steps.display: INEC: Federal & State elections  |  SIEC: Local Government Councils  |  Presidential petitions: Court of Appeal first (s. 239)
working: SIEC organises Local Government Council elections using INEC's voters' register (3rd Sched. Pt. II Item B para. 4).
Presidential election petitions start at the Court of Appeal (s. 239(1)), not the High Court or a State tribunal.
steps.narration: Two quick traps to dodge. First, INEC does not run local council elections inside states; each State Independent Electoral Commission handles those. Second, Presidential election disputes do not start at a normal tribunal or High Court. Under section two-thirty-nine, they go straight to the Court of Appeal first.

sources.where: ss. 197, 239(1), 285; 3rd Sched. Pt. I Item F, Pt. II Item B

steps.title: Universal voting at 18, spread rules, and independent electoral bodies
steps.display: Vote at 18  |  Run at 25 or 35  |  Win with votes + 25% spread  |  INEC & SIEC supervise
working: Election disputes go to the Court of Appeal (Presidential) or s. 285 tribunals under 21-day, 180-day, and 60-day deadlines.
steps.narration: Hold onto these four pillars of Nigerian elections. Citizens register at eighteen. Candidates qualify at twenty-five or thirty-five. Executive winners need wide national or state spread. Neutral commissions run the polls. Keep INEC and SIEC separate, and these questions become clear.

quickCheck.stem: Practice: Under section 239(1) of the 1999 Constitution, which court has original jurisdiction to hear and determine a petition challenging a Presidential election?

options.text: The Federal High Court
options.why: Wrong: the Federal High Court does not hear Presidential election petitions.

options.text: The Court of Appeal
options.why: Correct: section 239(1) grants the Court of Appeal exclusive original jurisdiction over Presidential and Vice-Presidential election petitions (with appeal to the Supreme Court).

options.text: The Supreme Court of Nigeria
options.why: Wrong: the Supreme Court hears appeals from the Court of Appeal under s. 233(2)(e), rather than acting as the court of first instance.

options.text: The Governorship Election Tribunal
options.why: Wrong: Governorship Election Tribunals under s. 285(2) hear only Governorship and Deputy Governorship petitions.

steps.title: Teams trying to drive the bus versus passengers speaking up
steps.display: Political party: contests elections to run government  |  Pressure group: persuades government to protect members' interests
working: Both grow out of citizens' freedom to associate (s. 40), yet only parties sponsor candidates for office.
steps.narration: Think of a town bus. Political parties compete to sit in the driver's seat. Trade unions and market associations sit as passengers urging the driver where to fix the road.

steps.title: Both rest on freedom of association, yet section 221 separates their roles
steps.display: Section 40: Right to form political parties, trade unions or associations  |  Section 221: Only political parties may canvass for votes or fund candidates
working: Every person may form or join a political party, trade union, or other association to protect their interests (s. 40).
No association other than a political party may canvass for votes or contribute to party or campaign funds (s. 221).
steps.narration: Why does the Constitution protect both parties and unions, then draw a sharp line between them? Because teachers' unions or doctors' guilds speak up on pay without wanting to run the country. Picture a market union endorsing better drains. Under section two-twenty-one, it still cannot donate campaign cash.

steps.title: Political parties must be national, open, democratic and Abuja-headquartered
steps.display: Sections 222–224: Open membership, no ethnic or religious symbols, Abuja HQ, 4-year elections, \frac{2}{3} States executive
working: Register national officers and party constitution with INEC (alterations within 30 days) (s. 222(a), (c)–(d)).
Open to all citizens; no ethnic or religious name, logo, or restriction; HQ in FCT Abuja (s. 222(b), (e)–(f)).
Democratic officer elections at least every 4 years; executive committee drawn from at least \frac{2}{3} of States and FCT (s. 223); aims conform to Chapter II (s. 224).
steps.narration: Nigeria once suffered bitter regional rivalries, so the Constitution blocks sectional parties. Suppose a group tries to register a party restricted to one town or one religion. INEC must reject it! A valid party needs an Abuja headquarters, open membership, national symbols, and leaders from two-thirds of states.

steps.title: Party finance bans foreign funds, arms and failed inactive parties
steps.display: Sections 225, 225A, 227: No foreign money, no party militias, and INEC can de-register non-performing parties
working: Parties submit annual asset, income, and spending statements to INEC; any foreign money received must be handed to INEC within 21 days (s. 225(1)–(4)).
Section 227 bans quasi-military organisations using physical force or coercion for political goals.
Section 225A (4th Alteration No. 9): INEC may de-register a party for breaching rules or failing to win 25% in 1 State or LGA or at least 1 ward, Assembly, or Council seat.
steps.narration: Why ban foreign cash and private guards for political parties? Because foreign donors or armed thugs could hijack Nigerian elections! Suppose an overseas group sends money to a Nigerian party. Under section two-twenty-five, the party must hand that money to INEC within twenty-one days. No party militias are allowed either.

steps.title: Candidates need party sponsorship, and defection rules guard mandates
steps.display: Sections 65(2)(b), 131(c): Party sponsorship required  |  Sections 68(1)(g), 109(1)(g): Defection vacates legislative seat unless party splits or merges
working: Qualifications for President, Governor, National Assembly, and State Assembly all require membership and sponsorship of a political party.
A lawmaker who switches parties before term's end loses their seat UNLESS the move resulted from a division in their old party or a merger.
steps.narration: In Nigeria, you cannot run as an independent candidate without a party ticket. And once elected, a lawmaker cannot jump ship casually. Picture a student elected on one club's manifesto who quits the next week. They lose their seat unless their old party genuinely split or merged.

steps.title: Read a worked question distinguishing parties from pressure groups
steps.display: Question: A national association of nurses lobbies the National Assembly for safer hospital shifts and also wants to fund a presidential candidate's campaign. Which action violates the 1999 Constitution?
working: Options: (A) Forming a nationwide nurses' association under section 40
(B) Sending petitions and memoranda to lawmakers on hospital conditions
(C) Contributing association funds directly to a candidate's election expenses
(D) Electing the association's own executive officers every two years
steps.narration: Let us trace a real-world scenario. Nurses form a union and speak up for better hospitals, which is healthy pressure-group work. Then they try to pay for an election campaign. Keep section forty and section two-twenty-one side by side as we examine each option.

steps.title: Eliminate lawful association activities and spot the s. 221 breach
steps.display: Wrong: (A), (B) and (D) are lawful  |  Right: (C) violates s. 221 ban on non-party campaign funding
working: Rule out (A): section 40 explicitly protects forming trade unions and interest associations.
Rule out (B): petitioning lawmakers to influence policy is a lawful core role of a pressure group.
Rule out (D): electing union leaders internally is ordinary association governance.
Correct: (C) Section 221 forbids any association other than a political party from canvassing for votes or contributing to party or candidate election expenses.
steps.narration: Check each choice cleanly. Option A is protected by section forty. Option B is normal lobbying of lawmakers. Option D is just internal union democracy. Option C crosses the constitutional boundary! Section two-twenty-one reserves campaign donations and vote canvassing strictly for registered political parties.

steps.title: Practice question on constitutional conditions for political parties
steps.display: Practice question: Which requirement must an association satisfy before functioning as a political party under sections 222–223 of the 1999 Constitution?
working: Options: (A) Maintain its headquarters in the State capital where it won the most votes
(B) Draw its executive committee from at least two-thirds of all States and the FCT
(C) Restrict its logo and membership to promote one regional culture
(D) Hold executive committee elections only once every eight years
steps.narration: Now test your memory with a JAMB-style practice question. Notice what sections two-twenty-two and two-twenty-three try to guarantee. They force every party to look national, stay democratic, and stay based in the capital. Check each option to see which one actually follows the Constitution.

steps.title: Check each condition against sections 222 and 223
steps.display: Right: (B) Federal character in party executive across ≥ \frac{2}{3} of States and FCT (s. 223(2)(b))
working: (A) Wrong: section 222(f) requires the party headquarters to be in the Federal Capital Territory, Abuja.
(B) Right: section 223(2)(b) requires executive committee members to come from at least two-thirds of all States and the FCT.
(C) Wrong: section 222(b) and (e) forbid ethnic, religious, or regional confinement in membership or logos.
(D) Wrong: section 223(2)(a) requires democratic officer elections at intervals not exceeding 4 years.
steps.narration: Three choices fail right away. Option A puts the headquarters in a state instead of Abuja. Option C turns the party into a sectional group, which section two-twenty-two bans. Option D stretches officer terms to eight years instead of four. Only B matches section two-twenty-three.

steps.title: Cross-carpeting does not always cost a lawmaker their seat
steps.display: General rule: Switching party = lose seat  |  Exception: Division in old party or merger (ss. 68(1)(g), 109(1)(g))
working: A legislator vacates the seat if they join another party mid-term without a division or merger in the sponsoring party.
steps.narration: Watch out for the 'always' trap on defection! Students hear that cross-carpeting costs a lawmaker their seat and stop reading. Look at the proviso in sections sixty-eight and one-zero-nine. If the old party genuinely divided into factions or merged with another party, the lawmaker keeps the seat.

steps.title: Freedom of association does not stop INEC from de-registering weak parties
steps.display: Section 40 proviso + Section 225A: Right to associate does not force INEC to keep unrecognised or non-winning parties
working: Section 40 expressly preserves INEC's powers over political parties it does not recognise.
Section 225A lets INEC de-register parties that fail minimum electoral or registration thresholds.
steps.narration: Some students think section forty means any club can stay on the ballot forever. Read the proviso at the end of section forty! It protects INEC's power to deny or withdraw recognition. Under section two-twenty-five A, parties that win zero seats or fail thresholds can be de-registered.

steps.title: Parties contest power nationally; pressure groups influence without contesting
steps.display: Section 40 protects both  |  Section 221 restricts voting campaigns to parties  |  Sections 222–227 enforce national reach
working: Parties must meet national registration, 4-year election, and finance rules; pressure groups lobby for interests.
steps.narration: Keep this contrast sharp. Both parties and pressure groups grow from section forty's right to associate. Yet only registered political parties can campaign, sponsor candidates, or receive election donations under section two-twenty-one. Remember Abuja headquarters, two-thirds spread, and no foreign cash, and you will ace this topic.

quickCheck.stem: Practice: Under section 225(3)–(4) of the 1999 Constitution, what must a Nigerian political party do if funds or assets are sent to it from outside Nigeria?

options.text: Deposit them in a special foreign reserve account until the next election
options.why: Wrong: section 225(3)(a)–(b) prohibits a political party from holding or retaining any funds or assets outside or from outside Nigeria.

options.text: Transfer them to the Independent National Electoral Commission within 21 days of receipt
options.why: Correct: section 225(4) requires any funds or assets remitted to a party from outside Nigeria to be paid over to INEC within 21 days with required details.

options.text: Spend them only on voter education and office rent
options.why: Wrong: a political party may not retain or spend foreign-remitted funds at all.

options.text: Share them equally among all registered political parties
options.why: Wrong: section 225(4) requires turning the funds over to INEC, not sharing them with rival parties.

lessons.title: Federalism in Nigeria and local government

steps.title: One big family house with rooms that run themselves
steps.display: Federal government (whole compound)  |  36 States + FCT (wings)  |  774 Local Councils (each room)
working: Nigeria shares power across three tiers so national unity and local needs work together.
steps.narration: Think of a large family compound. Everyone shares one main gate and generator, while each wing cleans its own parlour. Nigeria shares government duties across three levels the same way.

steps.title: Nigeria is a Federation of 36 States, the FCT and 774 local areas
steps.display: Sections 2 & 3: 1 Federation  |  36 States + FCT Abuja  |  768 LGAs + 6 FCT Area Councils = 774
working: Section 2(1)–(2): Nigeria is one indivisible and indissoluble Sovereign State and a Federation of States and a Federal Capital Territory.
Section 3(1) & (6): names 36 States, 768 local government areas, and 6 area councils in FCT (774 total in First Schedule).
steps.narration: Before asking who makes which rule, count the levels in Nigeria's structure. Section two says Nigeria is one indivisible federation. Section three lists thirty-six states, Abuja as the Federal Capital Territory, and seven hundred and seventy-four local councils in total. Notice how every tier is named directly in the Constitution.

sources.where: ss. 2(1)–(2), 3(1), 3(6); First Schedule Parts I & II

steps.title: Legislative powers split into Exclusive, Concurrent and Residual matters
steps.display: Section 4 & Second Schedule: Exclusive (Federal only)  |  Concurrent (Both; Federal prevails under s. 4(5))  |  Residual (States)
working: Exclusive List (2nd Sched. Pt. I, 68 items): only National Assembly legislates — e.g. defence, currency, foreign affairs, aviation, citizenship, census (s. 4(2)–(3)).
Concurrent List (2nd Sched. Pt. II): both National Assembly and State Houses of Assembly legislate — e.g. revenue allocation, antiquities, tax collection, local government elections.
Residual matters (not on either list): belong to State Houses of Assembly (s. 4(7)(a)); if a State Law clashes with a valid Federal Act, the Federal Act prevails (s. 4(5)).
steps.narration: How do thirty-six states avoid stepping on each other's toes? By dividing who writes which laws! Only the National Assembly prints currency or commands the army on the Exclusive List. Both federal and state assemblies share the Concurrent List, like revenue rules. Anything left off both lists goes to states.

sources.where: s. 4(2)–(7); Second Schedule Parts I & II

steps.title: Federal Character and Federation Account sharing manage diversity and funds
steps.display: Section 14(3): Federal Character  |  Section 162: Federation Account (≥ 13% derivation)
working: Federal Character (s. 14(3)–(4)): federal and state appointments must reflect Nigeria's diversity so no few States or ethnic groups dominate.
Federation Account (s. 162(1)–(3)): national revenues enter one pool shared among Federal, State, and Local Governments by National Assembly law, advised by RMAFC.
Section 162(2) proviso: natural-resource derivation must be at least 13%.
steps.narration: A huge diverse country needs fair sharing of jobs and money to stay united. Picture a family business sharing profits and manager posts across every branch. Section fourteen insists federal offices reflect all states, not a tiny clique. And section one-sixty-two pools revenue while giving resource-producing states at least thirteen percent.

sources.where: ss. 14(3)–(4), 162(1)–(3); 3rd Sched. Pt. I Items C & N

steps.title: Local government is constitutionally guaranteed with Fourth Schedule duties
steps.display: Section 7(1): Democratic local councils guaranteed  |  Fourth Schedule: Markets, parks, sanitation, primary schools & health
working: Section 7(1): democratic local government councils are guaranteed; States enact Laws for their structure, finance, and functions.

Fourth Schedule duties: markets, motor parks, cemeteries, naming streets, registration of births, deaths, and marriages, refuse disposal, and participating with the State in primary education and health care.
Finance: statutory allocations from the Federation Account (via State Joint Local Government Account, s. 162(5)–(6)) plus State revenue (s. 7(6)(b)) and local rates.
steps.narration: Why not handle every market stall and street drain from Abuja? Because Abuja is too far to inspect every borehole or motor park! Section seven guarantees elected local councils close to your home. Under the Fourth Schedule, they name streets, run markets, collect rates, and help run primary schools and clinics.

steps.title: Read a worked question on conflicting federal and state laws
steps.display: Question: Both the National Assembly and a State House of Assembly pass laws on a Concurrent List matter, and one clause in the State Law directly contradicts the Federal Act. Under section 4(5), what happens?
working: Options: (A) The State Law overrides the Federal Act inside that State
(B) Both laws become completely void and must be re-enacted
(C) The Federal Act prevails, and the State Law is void to the extent of the inconsistency
(D) Local Government Councils vote on which law to enforce
steps.narration: Let us work through a classic federalism clash. Both Lagos and Abuja are allowed to legislate on a Concurrent List topic, yet their two clauses collide. Which rule wins when they conflict? Keep section four subsection five in mind as we rule out the wrong options one by one.

steps.title: Apply section 4(5) to rule out wrong options
steps.display: Wrong: (A) State cannot override valid Federal Act  |  (B) Federal Act stays valid  |  (D) councils do not resolve statutory clashes
working: Rule out (A): section 4(5) gives priority to the valid National Assembly Act, not the State Law.
Rule out (B): the Federal Act remains valid, and even the rest of the State Law survives if not inconsistent.
Rule out (D): local councils have no constitutional authority to choose between federal and state statutes.
Correct: (C) Under section 4(5), the National Assembly law prevails and the State Law is void to the extent of the inconsistency.
steps.narration: Knock out the wrong choices carefully. Option A reverses the hierarchy. Option B goes too far, because the federal law and the harmless parts of the state law still stand! Option D hands the job to local councils instead of courts. That leaves C, matching section four subsection five.

steps.title: Practice question on Exclusive List versus Local Council duties
steps.display: Practice question: Which function belongs to a Local Government Council under the Fourth Schedule rather than the Exclusive Legislative List?
working: Options: (A) Currency, coinage and legal tender
(B) Defence and aviation
(C) Establishment and regulation of markets, motor parks and cemeteries
(D) Diplomatic representation and external affairs
steps.narration: Here is a practice question comparing the Exclusive List with local government jobs. Remember why the Fourth Schedule exists. Local councils handle everyday community services right in your neighbourhood, while Abuja handles national survival and foreign ties. Scan all four choices and spot the local community duty.

steps.title: Match each option to the Second or Fourth Schedule
steps.display: Right: (C) Markets, motor parks and cemeteries sit in Fourth Schedule paragraph 1(c), (e)
working: (A) Wrong: currency, coinage and legal tender is Item 15 on the Exclusive Legislative List.
(B) Wrong: defence (Item 17) and aviation (Item 3) are on the Exclusive Legislative List.
(C) Right: Fourth Schedule para. 1(c) and (e) assign cemeteries, markets, and motor parks to local government councils.
(D) Wrong: diplomatic representation (Item 20) and external affairs (Item 26) are on the Exclusive Legislative List.
steps.narration: Look how clear the match becomes! Printing naira notes is on the Exclusive List. Running the army, airports, and foreign embassies sits there too. Abuja handles all of those. Only C belongs to local councils. Caring for local markets, parks, and cemeteries sits in the Fourth Schedule.

steps.title: A State creating a new local council still needs National Assembly action
steps.display: Section 8(3) & (5)–(6): State Assembly passes the bill, then National Assembly amends section 3 and First Schedule
working: Until the National Assembly passes the consequential Act updating First Schedule under s. 8(5)–(6), the new council is not listed among the 774 constitutional areas.
steps.narration: Here is a trap students often miss about creating local governments. Yes, a State House of Assembly starts the process under section eight subsection three. Yet it cannot finish alone! Under subsections five and six, the National Assembly must pass an Act updating Nigeria's First Schedule list.

steps.title: Do not confuse Concurrent power with Residual power
steps.display: Concurrent (2nd Sched. Pt. II): Shared by Federal and States  |  Residual (s. 4(7)(a)): Left solely to States
working: If a topic is on neither the Exclusive List nor the Concurrent List, only State Houses of Assembly legislate on it (residual power).
If a topic is on the Concurrent List, both tiers may legislate, subject to s. 4(5) federal supremacy.
steps.narration: Keep 'concurrent' and 'residual' apart! Concurrent means running together, so both Abuja and the States can make laws on those listed items. Residual means what is left over. If a matter is missing from both constitutional lists, it belongs strictly to the State House of Assembly.

steps.title: Three tiers share power through lists, revenue pools and elected councils
steps.display: Exclusive (Federal)  |  Concurrent (Both, s. 4(5) Federal prevails)  |  Residual (States)  |  Local Councils (s. 7 & 4th Sched.)
working: Federal Character (s. 14(3)), Federation Account (s. 162, ≥ 13% derivation), and democratic local councils (s. 7) hold the federation together.
steps.narration: Carry this map of Nigerian federalism into the hall. Power splits across the Exclusive, Concurrent, and Residual baskets. Federal law prevails whenever clauses clash. Fair appointments, shared Federation Account funds, and elected local councils keep Nigeria's thirty-six states united while serving local communities.

quickCheck.stem: Practice: Under the proviso to section 162(2) of the 1999 Constitution, what minimum percentage must the revenue-allocation formula constantly reflect for derivation from natural resources?

options.text: Not less than 5 per cent
options.why: Wrong: 5 per cent is below the constitutional floor fixed in the proviso to section 162(2).

options.text: Not less than 10 per cent
options.why: Wrong: section 162(2) specifies a higher minimum than 10 per cent.

options.text: Not less than 13 per cent
options.why: Correct: the proviso to section 162(2) states that derivation shall be constantly reflected as 'not less than thirteen per cent' of revenue accruing to the Federation Account directly from natural resources.

options.text: Not less than 25 per cent
options.why: Wrong: 25 per cent is the electoral vote-spread threshold (ss. 134, 179), not the section 162(2) derivation floor.
